title: Correspondence between Asymptotic Quantum Many-Body Scars in Closed Systems and Diffusive Nambu-Goldstone Modes in Open Systems
authors: Masaya Kunimi, Taiki Haga, Masaya Nakagawa
abstract: Hydrodynamic relaxation in open quantum many-body systems can be understood in terms of diffusive Nambu--Goldstone (NG) modes associated with strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SWSSB). Here, we find a common structure underlying weak ergodicity breaking in closed quantum systems and diffusive hydrodynamics in open quantum systems. We establish a spectral correspondence between the parent Hamiltonian of rainbow quantum many-body scar (RQMBS) states in closed systems and the effective Lindbladian of strongly dissipative open systems with strong $U(1)$ symmetry and local charge-dephasing Lindblad operators. For broad classes of spin, fermionic, and bosonic systems, we construct asymptotic RQMBS (ARQMBS) states. Within the enlarged scar subspace, the parent Hamiltonian admits a local Rokhsar--Kivelson-type frustration-free decomposition. A single-mode variational construction gives an $O(k^2)$ upper bound on its lowest excitation energy and yields states satisfying the defining ARQMBS criteria: orthogonality, vanishing energy variance, and characteristic entanglement scaling. Under vectorization, RQMBS states are mapped to maximally mixed infinite-temperature states in fixed-charge sectors, which exhibit long-range SWSSB order under finite-density conditions. Assuming uniformly bounded positive transition rates, the effective Lindbladian has the same local projectors as the parent Hamiltonian but with positive transition-dependent weights, yielding two-sided spectral bounds and the same system-size scaling of their gaps. For uniform rates, the two operators are proportional to each other and their eigenmodes coincide. Therefore, an exact quadratic parent-Hamiltonian branch maps directly to a diffusive NG mode. Our results connect different mechanisms of slow relaxation in closed and open quantum many-body systems.
summary: This paper reveals a fundamental duality connecting slow, non-thermalizing states (Quantum Many-Body Scars) in closed quantum systems to diffusive Nambu-Goldstone modes in open systems. By establishing a spectral correspondence between the parent Hamiltonian and the effective Lindbladian, the authors unify the understanding of slow relaxation across different physical regimes. This has broad implications for understanding quantum dynamics in both isolated and dissipative environments.
main_problem: The paper establishes a deep theoretical correspondence between slow relaxation mechanisms in closed quantum systems (Quantum Many-Body Scars) and diffusive dynamics in open quantum systems (Nambu-Goldstone modes).
main_result: It shows that a common underlying structure links weak ergodicity breaking in closed systems to diffusive hydrodynamics in open systems, specifically mapping an exact quadratic parent-Hamiltonian branch to a diffusive NG mode.
method: The authors use spectral analysis, variational constructions, and the comparison between the parent Hamiltonian of the scar states and the effective Lindbladian of the open system.
model_or_system: The study considers general spin, fermionic, and bosonic systems, exemplified by models like the XXZ Hamiltonian on a two-leg ladder. The dynamics are governed by a closed system Hamiltonian and an open system Lindblad master equation.
key_observables: The key observables are the spectral properties: the gap scaling ($O(k^2)$) in the parent Hamiltonian for scars, and the decay rate $\lambda(k) \simeq Dk^2$ for the diffusive NG modes.
important_parameters: The correspondence holds under the assumption of strong U(1) symmetry and local charge-dephasing Lindblad operators, and for uniformly bounded positive transition rates.
main_assumptions: The correspondence is derived assuming the existence of asymptotic scar states and the applicability of the Lindblad formalism for the open system dynamics.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by first defining the scar states in closed systems, then analyzing the dynamics in open systems via the Lindbladian, and finally establishing the spectral correspondence between the two frameworks.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, unifying mathematical framework connecting two distinct physical phenomena—non-thermal scars in isolated systems and diffusive relaxation in open ones—using spectral theory.
